chapters.title: The question about saving life exposes the plan to destroy it
chapters.summary: Jesus enters a synagogue where a man has a withered hand. His opponents watch to see whether he will heal on the Sabbath. He asks whether the Sabbath is for doing good or harm, saving life or killing. They say nothing, and he heals the man. The Pharisees begin to plot his death. Crowds press on him, and he appoints twelve to be with him. Scribes say he drives out demons by their ruler. He says those who do God’s will are his family.
chapters.meaning: The watchers in verse 2 hope to accuse Jesus. Verse 4 puts a question to them with two pairs. Is the Sabbath for doing good or harm, for saving life or killing? They stay silent. He heals the man, which is the good. Verse 6 shows what they do on that same Sabbath. They go out and plan how to destroy him.

lds.text: The selected lesson uses the divided house saying to teach unity. How does the question about saving life expose the opponents’ plan?

chapters.historicalNote: Jesus asks whether Sabbath action should do good or harm, save life or kill. His opponents remain silent while he looks at them with anger and grief. The healed hand then meets their immediate plan to destroy him. Crowds from many regions seek the healing that this conflict threatens. The divided house argument answers the accusation that his freeing work serves the demons' ruler. The final family saying identifies those who do God's will rather than merely stay close.

chapters.title: Questions about hearing become fear inside the boat
chapters.summary: Jesus teaches a large crowd from a boat. A farmer sows seed on path, rock, thorns, and good soil. He explains the story to his disciples in private. A lamp is meant to be set on a stand. Seed grows by itself while the farmer sleeps. The Kingdom is like a tiny mustard seed that becomes a large plant. That evening a storm fills the boat while Jesus sleeps. He rebukes the wind, and the disciples are terrified.
chapters.meaning: The disciples have spent the day hearing about trust in a hidden Kingdom. That night the waves break into the boat. Verse 38 gives their question: does he not care that they are dying? They doubt his concern, not his power. He stills the storm and asks why they have no faith (verse 40). Verse 41 says they were then even more afraid. They ask who this can be.

lds.text: The selected lesson reads the storm account through peace during trouble. Why does fear remain after the disciples hear explanations and see the storm stop?

chapters.historicalNote: The seed stories ask how the word survives misunderstanding, pressure, and competing desires. A further growing seed story describes progress that the farmer cannot fully explain. The lamp image connects hidden things with their coming disclosure rather than permanent concealment. Jesus explains privately to disciples who still ask whether he cares during the storm. His command brings calm, but their fear remains as a new question about his identity. Hearing explanations therefore does not yet produce the confidence that their danger requires.

chapters.title: One healing interrupts another urgent request
chapters.summary: Jesus crosses the lake and frees a man held by many demons. The man had lived among tombs, and no chain could hold him. The townspeople beg Jesus to leave. Jairus, a synagogue leader, begs him to come to his dying daughter. On the way a woman who has bled for twelve years touches his cloak. She is healed, and Jesus stops to find her. Word comes that the girl has died. Jesus takes her hand, and she gets up.
chapters.meaning: A leader’s daughter is dying, and every moment counts. A woman in the crowd touches Jesus and is healed at once (verse 29). He could have kept walking. He stops and asks who touched him (verse 30). She comes forward in fear and tells him everything. Verse 34 calls her “Daughter” and sends her away in peace. She receives his attention as well as her cure, while Jairus waits.

lds.text: Why does Jesus stop to hear the woman while Jairus waits?

chapters.historicalNote: The man among the tombs first receives release that makes the surrounding people afraid. Jesus sends him home to tell about mercy while the people request Jesus' departure. Across the sea, Jairus' urgent request becomes a journey interrupted by the bleeding woman's touch. Her twelve years of suffering end before news arrives that the ruler's daughter has died. Jesus addresses her as daughter, making her account visible rather than leaving the touch anonymous. He then raises the twelve-year-old girl and orders food, joining restored life with ordinary care.

chapters.title: The loaves should have changed the disciples' response to the sea
chapters.summary: Jesus teaches in his home town, and the people take offense. He sends the twelve out two by two. Herod has John the Baptist beheaded after a rash promise at a feast. The twelve return, and Jesus takes them aside to rest. A crowd follows, and he feeds five thousand with five loaves and two fish. That night he walks on the sea toward the disciples’ boat. They are terrified, and he gets in with them. People bring the sick wherever he goes.
chapters.meaning: The disciples have just handed out bread to thousands (verses 41–43). Hours later they see Jesus on the water and cry out in fear. Verse 52 explains their reaction. They had not understood about the loaves. The feeding should have shown them who was with them. Their hearts were hardened. In Mark the people closest to Jesus are often slow to see.

lds.text: What should the disciples have understood from the loaves before the sea encounter?

chapters.historicalNote: The disciples' return from traveling work surrounds the account of John's death at Herod's meal. Herod's regret does not prevent an order made to satisfy his promises and guests. Jesus' gathering instead answers people whom he sees as sheep without a shepherd. Teaching and divided loaves provide care where the disciples first propose sending the crowd away. Their later fear on the sea follows that meal but fails to learn from it. Mark explicitly connects their amazement with hardened hearts and misunderstanding about the loaves.

chapters.title: A sacred gift claim can hide neglected parents
chapters.summary: Pharisees ask why Jesus’s disciples eat with unwashed hands. He says they honor God with their lips and hold to human tradition. The law says to honor father and mother. They let a man declare his goods “Corban,” a gift to God. He then gives his parents nothing. Jesus says evil comes from within, out of the heart. He heals a foreign woman’s daughter. He opens the ears and mouth of a deaf man.
chapters.meaning: “Corban” in verse 11 means something pledged to God. A man could say this about the support he owed his parents. Verse 12 states the result. He is then not allowed to do anything for his father or mother. A religious vow cancels a plain commandment. Jesus says this makes God’s word void (verse 13). The example shows how piety can excuse neglect.

lds.text: How can calling property sacred become a refusal to help parents?

chapters.historicalNote: The washing dispute leads Jesus to an example about support owed to parents. Calling resources a gift to God can become an excuse to refuse that support. Jesus therefore challenges a practice that undermines the command it claims to serve. His explanation places harmful conduct within the heart rather than food entering the body. The foreign woman's reply then presses a food image toward help for her daughter. A deaf man's restored speech ends the chapter with praise spreading despite the silence command.

chapters.title: Partial sight stands beside partial understanding
chapters.summary: Jesus feeds four thousand people with seven loaves. Pharisees ask for a sign, and he refuses. In the boat the disciples worry that they have one loaf. He asks whether they still do not understand. At Bethsaida he heals a blind man in two stages. He asks who they say he is, and Peter calls him the Christ. Jesus says he must suffer, and Peter rebukes him. Jesus says his followers must take up their cross.
chapters.meaning: This is the only healing in the Gospels done in two steps. After the first touch the man sees people like walking trees (verse 24). After the second he sees clearly (verse 25). Mark places the story between two scenes of poor sight. The disciples fail to understand the loaves (verses 17–21). Peter then names Jesus rightly and rejects his suffering (verses 29–32). Their sight is also partial.

lds.text: How does the two-stage healing sit beside Peter’s incomplete understanding?

chapters.historicalNote: The second feeding answers hunger after the crowd has stayed three days. The disciples later worry about missing bread despite remembering both feedings and their remaining baskets. Jesus' questions connect that failure with unseeing eyes and unhearing ears. The blind man's healing then takes two stages before his sight becomes clear. Peter's confession likewise names the Christ before he rejects the announced suffering. Recognizing the title leaves his understanding incomplete until following includes the costly path Jesus describes.

chapters.title: The father's request admits the weakness that disciples conceal
chapters.summary: Jesus is changed in appearance on a mountain before three disciples. A voice from the cloud tells them to listen to him. Below, a father has brought a son whom the disciples could not heal. The father asks Jesus to help if he can. Jesus says all things are possible for one who believes. The father cries that he believes and asks help for his unbelief. Jesus heals the boy and again foretells his death. The disciples argue about who is greatest.
chapters.meaning: The father’s cry in verse 24 holds two things together. He believes, and he knows his belief is weak. He says both aloud and asks for help. The disciples behave differently in this chapter. They do not understand and are afraid to ask (verse 32). They argue about rank and fall silent when questioned (verse 34). The father admits his weakness, and they hide theirs.

lds.text: How does the father’s request differ from the disciples’ silence about their fears?

chapters.historicalNote: The mountain voice directs the frightened disciples to listen to the beloved Son. They still question what rising from death means as they return below. A distressed father then names his son's danger and the disciples' failure to help. His request admits both belief and unbelief rather than presenting confidence without weakness. The disciples later fear asking about death and quietly argue about which one is greatest. Jesus answers their rank concern through service and a child placed in their midst.

chapters.title: The same question reveals different desires in two requests
chapters.summary: Jesus teaches about marriage and blesses the children. A rich man asks how to inherit eternal life and leaves in sorrow. Jesus foretells his death a third time. James and John ask to sit at his right and left in glory. He says whoever would be great must be a servant. At Jericho a blind beggar named Bartimaeus cries out to him. Jesus asks what he wants. He asks to see, receives his sight, and follows Jesus.

lds.text: The selected lesson studies the wealthy man’s question about following Jesus. How do the two answers to the same question reveal different desires?

chapters.title: The fig tree surrounds a dispute about the temple's purpose
chapters.summary: Jesus rides into Jerusalem on a colt, and people shout “Hosanna.” The next day he finds a fig tree with leaves and no fruit. He says no one will eat from it again. He drives the buyers and sellers out of the temple. He says God’s house should be a house of prayer for all nations. The following morning the fig tree has withered. He teaches about faith, prayer, and forgiveness. The leaders ask by what authority he does these things.
chapters.meaning: Mark wraps the temple scene inside the fig tree story. The tree is cursed in verses 12–14 and found dead in verses 20–21. Between them Jesus stops the temple’s trade. Verse 17 quotes Isaiah 56:7 and Jeremiah 7:11. The house was meant for the prayer of all nations. A tree with leaves and no fruit frames that charge. The show of life without its purpose is what is judged.

lds.text: How do the tree scenes frame the temple interruption?

chapters.historicalNote: Jesus first enters the temple, looks around, and leaves because evening has come. The next day's fruitless tree appears before his return to interrupt buying and selling. His teaching joins a house of prayer for all nations with the accusation of robbery. A later sight of the withered tree places that interruption between two linked tree scenes. Prayer and forgiveness then receive attention before the authorities challenge his right to act. Their refusal to answer his question about John reflects fear of the people watching.

chapters.title: The widow's whole living follows a warning about consumed houses

Jesus names love of God and love of neighbor. He warns about scribes who love honor and devour widows’ houses. He sits and watches people put money in the temple treasury. Rich people give large sums. A poor widow gives two small coins, all she has.
chapters.meaning: Verse 40 warns of scribes who “devour widows’ houses.” The next scene shows a widow at the treasury. Verse 44 says she gave everything she had to live on. Jesus praises the size of her gift measured by her means. The warning just before should stay in the reader’s mind. A system that takes a widow’s last coins is also in view. The next chapter opens with the temple’s coming ruin (13:2).

lds.text: How does the warning about widows’ houses affect reading the widow’s gift?

chapters.historicalNote: The vineyard story provokes opponents who recognize themselves in the accused farmers. Tax and resurrection questions follow before one scribe answers Jesus with understanding about love. That exchange prevents the chapter from making every scribe an identical opponent. Jesus then warns against honored religious figures who consume widows' houses while displaying long prayers. The poor widow gives all she has to live on after that warning. Her small coins expose the difference between surplus giving and one's whole living.

chapters.title: The warning to watch does not supply a predictable hour
chapters.summary: A disciple admires the temple’s great stones. Jesus says not one will be left on another. Four disciples ask when this will happen. He warns of deceivers, wars, earthquakes, and trials before councils. They must flee when they see the desolating sacrilege. The Son of Man will come in the clouds. No one knows the day or the hour. They must stay awake, like servants whose master is away.
chapters.meaning: The disciples ask for timing and a sign (verse 4). Verse 32 says no one knows the day, not even the Son. So the chapter cannot be used as a timetable. Verse 34 gives a different picture. A man leaves home and gives each servant his work. The doorkeeper is told to watch. The command to stay awake is a command to keep at one’s task.

lds.text: What work remains possible when the day and hour stay unknown?

chapters.historicalNote: A disciple admires temple buildings before Jesus announces their complete destruction. Four disciples ask privately about the time and sign of those events. Jesus warns about deception, trials, divided families, and the particular hardships of hurried flight. The coming Son of Man follows images of shaken skies and gathered chosen people. Yet the day and hour remain unknown even to the Son within this saying. The doorkeeper story turns that uncertainty into watching while each servant has assigned work.

chapters.title: The woman's understood gift contrasts with failed promises
chapters.summary: The leaders look for a way to arrest Jesus. At Bethany a woman pours costly perfume on his head. Some scold her, and Jesus defends her. Judas agrees to betray him. Jesus eats the Passover and gives the bread and the cup. In Gethsemane he prays in anguish while his friends sleep. He is arrested, and all the disciples run. The council condemns him, and Peter denies him three times.
chapters.meaning: Some at the table call the woman’s gift a waste (verses 4–5). Verse 8 gives Jesus’s reading of it. She has done what she could and prepared his body for burial. She alone acts as if his death is near. The disciples make promises in this chapter. Peter swears he will die before denying him (verse 31). By verse 50 they have all fled.

lds.text: How does the woman’s action differ from the disciples’ promises?

chapters.historicalNote: An unnamed woman anoints Jesus while critics call the costly ointment a waste. Jesus identifies preparation for burial and promises remembrance of her action. Judas' bargain and the shared meal then place betrayal inside the circle of the twelve. The garden's repeated sleeping reveals the gap between Peter's promises and his ability to watch. Arrest ends with flight, including an unnamed young man who abandons his linen covering. Peter's denials finally match the warned pattern when the rooster crows a second time.

chapters.title: Mocked kingship becomes recognition beside the cross
chapters.summary: The council hands Jesus to Pilate. Pilate offers to release him, and the crowd chooses Barabbas. Soldiers dress Jesus in purple and mock him as king. Simon of Cyrene is made to carry his cross. He is crucified with two robbers, and passersby mock him. Darkness covers the land, and he cries out and dies. The temple curtain tears in two. A Roman officer says this man was the Son of God.
chapters.meaning: Mockers tell Jesus to come down from the cross so they can believe (verse 32). He does not come down. Verse 39 says the officer saw how he died. The officer then calls him Son of God. This is the first human in Mark to say so. He is a foreign soldier at an execution. Recognition comes at the death, not through an escape from it.

lds.text: Why does the officer’s recognition follow death rather than escape from the cross?

chapters.historicalNote: Pilate recognizes envy yet releases Barabbas and hands Jesus over to satisfy the crowd. Soldiers turn the royal title into mockery through clothing, thorns, and a reed. The written accusation keeps that same title visible during the execution. Jesus' abandonment cry remains unanswered by the people who misunderstand it as calling Elijah. The officer's recognition follows Jesus' death rather than a display that escapes the cross. Women watch, and two named Marys then see where Joseph places the body.

chapters.title: The message names Peter after his denial and the disciples' flight
chapters.summary: After the Sabbath three women bring spices to the tomb. They wonder who will roll away the stone. They find it moved and a young man in white inside. He says Jesus has risen and is not there. They must tell his disciples and Peter that he goes ahead to Galilee. The women flee, trembling and afraid. The longer ending tells of Jesus appearing to Mary Magdalene and others. He sends the eleven into all the world.
chapters.meaning: The disciples fled at the arrest (14:50). Peter denied Jesus three times (14:66–72). Verse 7 sends a message to “his disciples and Peter.” Peter is named on his own. The one who failed most publicly is not left out. The message also promises a meeting in Galilee, as Jesus said (14:28). The first word to those who ran is an invitation back.

lds.text: The selected lesson teaches resurrection through the Gospel accounts. Why does the tomb message name Peter after his denial?

chapters.historicalNote: The women buy spices to tend the body they saw placed in the tomb. A young man instead announces resurrection and directs them toward a promised meeting in Galilee. Naming Peter keeps his denial from excluding him from the message to the disciples. Fear initially silences the women despite that instruction. The WEB text continues with appearances, disbelief, and a command to carry the message worldwide. Black discusses competing endings after verse eight, while this edition retains verses nine through twenty.

steps.title: Questions about hearing become fear inside the boat
steps.text: The disciples have spent the day hearing about trust in a hidden Kingdom. That night the waves break into the boat. Verse 38 gives their question: does he not care that they are dying? They doubt his concern, not his power. He stills the storm and asks why they have no faith (verse 40). Verse 41 says they were then even more afraid. They ask who this can be.

steps.title: Partial sight stands beside partial understanding
steps.text: This is the only healing in the Gospels done in two steps. After the first touch the man sees people like walking trees (verse 24). After the second he sees clearly (verse 25). Mark places the story between two scenes of poor sight. The disciples fail to understand the loaves (verses 17–21). Peter then names Jesus rightly and rejects his suffering (verses 29–32). Their sight is also partial.
